chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Dashwood family had lived in Sussex for a very long time. They owned a large estate and made their home at Norland Park, in the middle of their land. For many generations they had lived there with a respectability that won the general approval of everyone they knew in the neighbourhood. The estate's last owner was an unmarried man who lived to a great age. For many years his sister had kept him company and managed his household. Her death, ten years before his own, changed his home considerably. To fill the gap she left, he invited his nephew, Mr. Henry Dashwood, and his family to live with him. This nephew was the legal heir to Norland, and the person he intended to leave it to. With his nephew and niece and their children around him, the old gentleman passed his days in comfort, growing steadily more attached to them all. Mr. and Mrs. Henry Dashwood constantly attended to his wishes, out of real kindness as well as an interest in their future inheritance. They gave him every substantial comfort his age allowed, while the children's cheerfulness brought a fresh enjoyment to his life.

Mr. Henry Dashwood had a son by his first marriage and three daughters by his present wife. His son, a dependable, respectable young man, was already well provided for. His mother's fortune had been considerable, and half of it had passed to him when he came of age. A marriage of his own soon afterwards added still more to his wealth. Inheriting Norland was therefore much less important to him than it was to his sisters. Apart from whatever their father's inheritance might bring them, the girls could expect very little money. Their mother had no fortune, and their father had only seven thousand pounds that he could freely dispose of. The other half of his first wife's money was also reserved for her son; Henry had only the right to its income during his lifetime.

The old gentleman died. His will was read and, like almost every will, caused as much disappointment as satisfaction. He was neither unfair nor ungrateful enough to leave the estate away from his nephew—but the conditions he attached to the inheritance destroyed half its value. Mr. Dashwood had wanted it more for his wife and daughters than for himself or his son. Yet it was secured to his son and his son's son, a child of four, on terms that left him unable to provide for those he loved most and who most needed help. He could neither raise money against the estate nor sell its valuable timber for their benefit. Everything was tied up for the child. On occasional visits to Norland with his parents, this little boy had won his uncle's affection with attractions by no means rare in children of two or three: indistinct speech, a firm determination to get his own way, plenty of sly little tricks, and a great deal of noise. These had outweighed all the years of attention the old gentleman had received from his niece and her daughters. He had no wish to be unkind, however. As a sign of his affection for the three girls, he left each of them a thousand pounds.

At first Mr. Dashwood was bitterly disappointed. But he was naturally cheerful and hopeful, and could reasonably expect to live for many years. By keeping his expenses low, he might save a considerable amount from the income of an estate already large and capable of improvement almost at once. Yet the fortune that had taken so long to reach him remained his for only a year. He outlived his uncle by no more than twelve months, and all that was left for his widow and daughters, including the recent legacies, was ten thousand pounds.

As soon as his condition was known to be dangerous, his son was sent for. With all the strength and urgency his illness allowed, Mr. Dashwood entrusted the welfare of his son's stepmother and sisters to his care.

Mr. John Dashwood did not share the rest of the family's depth of feeling. Still, such an appeal, made at such a moment, moved him, and he promised to do everything he could to make them comfortable. The assurance put his father's mind at rest. Mr. John Dashwood then had time to consider how much, in prudence, he could actually afford to do for them.

He was not a bad-hearted young man, unless being rather cold-hearted and rather selfish amounts to being bad-hearted. In general, people respected him, since he behaved properly in carrying out his everyday duties. A kinder wife might have made him more worthy of respect still; she might even have made him kind himself. He had married very young and was extremely fond of his wife. Mrs. John Dashwood, however, was an exaggerated version of her husband, with an even narrower mind and greater selfishness.

When he made the promise to his father, he privately intended to add a thousand pounds to each of his sisters' fortunes. At that moment he genuinely believed he could afford it. The prospect of four thousand a year on top of his existing income, together with the remaining half of his mother's fortune, warmed his heart and made generosity seem possible. “Yes, he would give them three thousand pounds. It would be a generous, handsome gift! It would be enough to set their minds completely at ease. Three thousand pounds! Even so considerable a sum could be spared with very little inconvenience.” He thought about it throughout that day and for several days afterwards, without regretting his decision.

The funeral was scarcely over when Mrs. John Dashwood arrived with her child and their servants, having given her mother-in-law no warning that she intended to come. Nobody could question her right to do so: the house had belonged to her husband from the instant of his father's death. But that only made her lack of tact more glaring. Any woman in Mrs. Dashwood's position, with ordinary feelings, would have found it deeply unpleasant. Her own sense of honour was so acute, and her generosity so romantic, that an offence of this sort, whoever committed or suffered it, provoked in her a disgust that nothing could shake. Mrs. John Dashwood had never been liked by her husband's family. Until now, however, she had lacked an opportunity to show just how little she could consider other people's comfort when circumstances suited her.

Mrs. Dashwood felt this ungracious behaviour so keenly, and despised her daughter-in-law so thoroughly for it, that she would have left the house for ever the moment the other woman arrived. Her eldest daughter pleaded with her to consider first whether leaving was the proper course. Then her tender love for all three of her children persuaded her to stay, and for their sake to avoid a quarrel with their brother.

Elinor, the eldest daughter whose advice had such influence, had a strong understanding and a calm judgment. Though only nineteen, she was fitted to advise her mother. Often, to everyone's benefit, she could check the impulsive enthusiasm that would otherwise have led Mrs. Dashwood into unwise decisions. She had an excellent heart: she was affectionate by nature and felt things deeply. But she knew how to control her feelings—a lesson her mother had still to learn, and one of her sisters had decided she would never be taught.

In many ways Marianne was just as able as Elinor. She was intelligent and thoughtful, but passionate about everything; neither sorrow nor joy could ever be moderate with her. She was generous, lovable, engaging—everything, in fact, except cautious. The resemblance between her and her mother was extraordinarily strong.

Elinor watched her sister's excessive emotional sensitivity with concern; Mrs. Dashwood prized and encouraged it. Mother and daughter now urged each other on in the intensity of their grief. The anguish that had first overwhelmed them was deliberately revived, sought out, and created afresh again and again. They surrendered themselves entirely to sorrow, dwelling on every thought that could make them more miserable and resolving never to accept comfort in the future. Elinor too was deeply grieved, but she could still struggle against her suffering and make an effort. She could discuss matters with her brother, welcome her sister-in-law on her arrival and give her the attention due to her. She could also try to stir her mother to the same effort, and encourage her to show the same restraint.

Margaret, the remaining sister, was cheerful and good-natured. But she had already absorbed a good deal of Marianne's romantic thinking without much of her good sense. At thirteen, she therefore showed little promise of matching either of her sisters when she was older.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: Mrs. John Dashwood now established herself as the mistress of Norland, reducing her mother-in-law and sisters-in-law to the position of guests. She did, however, treat them with a quiet politeness. Her husband showed them as much kindness as he could feel for anyone outside himself, his wife, and their child. He urged them, with some real earnestness, to regard Norland as their home. Mrs. Dashwood could think of no better plan than to remain there until she found a house nearby that would suit her, and accepted his invitation.

Staying where everything recalled former happiness was exactly what her present state of mind required. When cheerful, nobody could be more cheerful than she was, or enjoy more fully that hopeful anticipation of happiness which is itself a kind of happiness. But in grief her imagination must carry her just as far: she was as completely beyond comfort in sorrow as she was beyond any taint of unhappiness in joy.

Mrs. John Dashwood thoroughly disapproved of her husband's plans for his sisters. Taking three thousand pounds from their dear little boy's fortune would impoverish him to a dreadful extent. She begged her husband to reconsider. How could he justify to himself robbing his child—his only child, too—of such an enormous sum? And what possible claim on his generosity could the Miss Dashwoods possibly have on so much generosity? They were only his half-sisters, which, in her opinion, counted as no relationship whatsoever. Everyone knew that affection was never expected between a man's children by different marriages. Why should he ruin himself and their poor little Harry by giving all his money away to his half-sisters?
“My father's last request,” her husband answered, “was that I should help his widow and daughters.”

“I dare say he had no idea what he was saying. Ten to one he was delirious at the time. If he had been in his right mind, he could never have thought of asking you to take half your fortune away from your own child.”

“He named no particular amount, my dear Fanny. He only asked, in general terms, that I should help them and make their circumstances more comfortable than he was able to do. Perhaps it would have been just as well if he had left the matter entirely to me. He could hardly have imagined that I would neglect them. But since he asked for a promise, I could scarcely refuse to give it—or at least, that was what I thought then. In any case, I made the promise and must keep it. We must do something for them when they leave Norland and establish a home of their own.”

“Very well, then, do something for them. But that something need not amount to three thousand pounds. Remember,” she went on, “once you have parted with the money, you can never get it back. Your sisters will marry, and it will be lost for ever. Now, if it could eventually come back to our poor little boy—”

“Well, certainly,” her husband said with great seriousness, “that would make a considerable difference. Harry may one day regret our having given away so large a sum. Suppose he has a great many children, for example. The extra money would then be extremely useful.”
“Yes, it certainly would.”
“Perhaps it would be better for everyone, then, to reduce the sum by half. Five hundred pounds each would still make an enormous addition to their fortunes!”
“Oh! Enormous hardly describes it! What brother anywhere would do half as much, even for sisters who were really his sisters! And these are only half-sisters! But you have such a generous nature!”

“I should not like to do anything mean,” he answered. “In such matters, one would rather give too much than too little. At least nobody could say I had not done enough for them. Even they themselves could hardly expect anything more.”
“Who knows what they may expect?” said his wife. “But their expectations are not our concern. The question is what you can afford.”

“Certainly. And I believe I can afford five hundred pounds for each of them. Even without any addition from me, they will each have about three thousand pounds when their mother dies. That is a very comfortable fortune for a young woman.”

“Indeed it is. In fact, it occurs to me that they need no addition whatever. There will be ten thousand pounds to share among them. If they marry, they are sure to do well; and if they remain single, the interest on ten thousand pounds will let them all live together very comfortably.”

“That is quite true. Perhaps, on the whole, it would be wiser to do something for their mother during her lifetime instead of giving money to the girls. I mean some sort of annuity, a regular yearly payment. My sisters would benefit from it as much as she would. A hundred pounds a year would make them all perfectly comfortable.”
His wife, however, did not agree to this proposal without a little hesitation.
“Certainly,” she said, “it is better than handing over fifteen hundred pounds at once. But if Mrs. Dashwood lives another fifteen years, we shall have been thoroughly taken in.”
“Fifteen years, my dear Fanny! One could hardly value her remaining life at even half that number.”

“Certainly not. But you will notice that people always live for ever when someone has to pay them an annuity. And she is strong and healthy and barely forty. An annuity is a serious undertaking: it comes round again every single year, and there is no way of getting rid of it. You do not realise what you are committing yourself to. I know a great deal about the trouble these payments cause. My father's will burdened my mother with annuities for three old retired servants, and it is astonishing how disagreeable she found it. They had to be paid twice a year; then there was the trouble of getting the money to them. Then someone said one of them had died, and afterwards it turned out that nothing of the sort had happened. My mother was quite sick of the whole business. With these endless claims upon her income, she said it was not her own. It was particularly unkind of my father, because otherwise she could have done exactly as she pleased with all the money, without any restrictions. It has given me such a horror of annuities that nothing in the world would persuade me to commit myself to paying one.”

“It is certainly unpleasant,” Mr. Dashwood replied, “to have that sort of annual drain on one's income. As your mother so rightly says, one's fortune is no longer one's own. Being obliged to pay a fixed sum whenever the rents come in is hardly desirable. It deprives one of independence.”

“Exactly. And after all that, you get no thanks. They know the money is guaranteed, so you are merely doing what they expect, and they feel no gratitude whatever. If I were you, I would make sure that everything I did was entirely at my own discretion. I would not promise them any yearly allowance. Some years it may be most inconvenient to take a hundred pounds, or even fifty, out of our own expenses.”

“I believe you are right, my love. It will be better to leave annuities out of the question. Whatever I give them from time to time will help far more than a yearly allowance. If they knew they had a larger income, they would simply live more expensively, and at the year's end they would not be sixpence better off. Yes, this will certainly be the best arrangement. A gift of fifty pounds now and again will keep them from ever being short of money, and I think that will more than fulfil my promise to my father.”

“Of course it will. Indeed, to tell the truth, I am convinced your father never intended you to give them money at all. I dare say he only meant the sort of help that anyone might reasonably expect: finding them a comfortable little house, for example, helping them move their belongings, and sending presents of fish and game and so on when they are in season. I would stake my life on his meaning nothing more. It would have been very strange and unreasonable if he had. Just consider, my dear Mr. Dashwood, how exceedingly comfortable your stepmother and her daughters can be on the interest from seven thousand pounds. Besides that, each girl has a thousand pounds of her own, bringing her fifty pounds a year, and naturally she will pay her mother for her board out of that. Altogether they will have five hundred pounds a year between them. What in the world could four women need beyond that? They will live so cheaply! Their household costs will be next to nothing. They will have no carriage, no horses, hardly any servants. They will entertain nobody and have no expenses of any kind! Just imagine their comfort! Five hundred a year! I cannot think how they will manage to spend even half of it. As for giving them more, the idea is quite absurd. They will be far better placed to give something to you.”

“Upon my word,” Mr. Dashwood said, “I believe you are entirely right. My father certainly cannot have meant anything beyond what you describe. I see it clearly now. I shall keep my promise to the letter by offering precisely those acts of help and kindness. When my mother moves to another house, I shall gladly do whatever I can to make the move easy for her. Perhaps a small gift of furniture would also be welcome then.”

“Certainly,” Mrs. John Dashwood answered. “Still, there is one thing to remember. When your father and mother came to Norland, they sold the furniture at Stanhill, but kept all the china, silver, and household linen. Those things have now been left to your mother. Her house will therefore be almost fully equipped as soon as she takes possession of it.”
“That is certainly an important consideration. A valuable inheritance indeed! Though some of the silver would have made a very welcome addition to what we have here.”

“Yes, and the breakfast china is twice as fine as the set belonging to this house. Far too fine, in my opinion, for any place they will ever be able to afford. But there it is. Your father thought of nobody but them. And I must say that you owe him no particular gratitude, or special regard for his wishes. We both know perfectly well that, if he could have done so, he would have left them almost everything he possessed.”

There was no resisting this argument. It supplied whatever firmness his intentions still lacked. He finally decided that doing anything beyond the neighbourly favours his wife had described for his father's widow and children would be entirely unnecessary, if not positively improper.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: Mrs. Dashwood stayed at Norland for several months. This was not because she had no wish to leave once familiar places stopped arousing the violent feelings they had stirred at first. As her spirits recovered, and she became able to do something besides deepen her grief with melancholy memories, she grew impatient to go. She searched tirelessly for a suitable home near Norland, since moving far from that beloved place was out of the question. But she heard of no house that satisfied both her own ideas of comfort and ease and her eldest daughter's caution. Elinor's steadier judgment rejected several houses her mother would have chosen because they were too large for their income.

Her husband had told Mrs. Dashwood of his son's solemn promise to help them, a promise that had comforted his final thoughts. She no more questioned its sincerity than he had. Thinking of her daughters, she looked forward to it with satisfaction; for herself, she was certain that far less than seven thousand pounds would maintain her in affluence. She was glad for their brother too, for the evidence of goodness in his own heart. She blamed herself for having judged him unfairly before, when she had thought him incapable of generosity. His considerate behaviour towards her and his sisters convinced her that he cared deeply about their welfare. For a long time she placed complete confidence in the generosity of his intentions.

The contempt she had felt for her daughter-in-law almost from the beginning of their acquaintance grew considerably during the six months they lived together, as she came to know her character better. Perhaps, despite all Mrs. Dashwood's concern for politeness and all her affection for her children, the two women could not have managed so long under one roof. But a particular circumstance arose that made her daughters' continued stay at Norland seem, in Mrs. Dashwood's opinion, more desirable than ever.

That circumstance was a growing affection between her eldest daughter and Mrs. John Dashwood's brother. He was a pleasant, well-mannered young man who had been introduced to them soon after his sister took over Norland, and had since spent most of his time there.

Some mothers might have encouraged the friendship out of self-interest: Edward Ferrars was the eldest son of a man who had died very wealthy. Others might have discouraged it out of caution, since apart from a small sum, his entire fortune depended on his mother's wishes. Neither consideration influenced Mrs. Dashwood. It was enough that he seemed kind, that he loved her daughter, and that Elinor liked him in return. All her principles opposed the idea that unequal fortunes should separate two people drawn together by similar temperaments. As for anyone failing to appreciate Elinor's worth once they knew her, that was beyond her imagination.

Edward Ferrars had no particular elegance of appearance or manner to recommend him. He was not handsome, and his manners became pleasing only as one got to know him. He was too unsure of himself to show his qualities to advantage. But once his natural shyness wore off, everything in his behaviour suggested an open and affectionate heart. He had a sound understanding, strengthened considerably by his education. Neither his talents nor his inclinations, however, suited the ambitions of his mother and sister. They wanted him to become distinguished—as what, they scarcely knew. Somehow or other, he must cut an impressive figure in the world. His mother hoped to interest him in politics, secure him a seat in parliament, or see him associated with the great men of the day. Mrs. John Dashwood shared those wishes. Meanwhile, until one of those greater blessings arrived, the sight of him driving a fashionable barouche carriage would have satisfied her ambition. But Edward cared neither for great men nor for barouches. All he wanted was a comfortable home and a quiet private life. Fortunately, his younger brother showed more promise.

Edward had spent several weeks in the house before Mrs. Dashwood paid him much attention. Her grief at that time made her indifferent to the people and things around her. She noticed only that he was quiet and did not intrude, and liked him for that. He never interrupted her misery with conversation at the wrong moment. What first made her observe him more closely, and approve of him more warmly, was a chance remark Elinor made one day about how different he was from his sister. Nothing could have recommended him more powerfully to her mother.
“That is enough,” she said. “It is enough to tell me he is unlike Fanny. That suggests every possible good quality. I love him already.”
“I believe you will like him,” Elinor said, “once you know him better.”
“Like him!” her mother answered, smiling. “I have no favourable feelings that stop short of love.”
“You might respect him.”
“I have never understood how respect and love could be separated.”

Mrs. Dashwood now made an effort to know him. Her warmth soon overcame his reserve. She quickly recognised all his good qualities; perhaps her conviction that he cared for Elinor sharpened her insight. But she was genuinely certain of his worth. Even his quiet manner, so contrary to all her settled notions of how a young man ought to behave, ceased to seem uninteresting once she knew he had a warm heart and an affectionate nature.
The moment she noticed any sign of love in his behaviour towards Elinor, she treated their deep attachment as an established fact and expected a wedding very soon.
“In a few months, my dear Marianne,” she said, “Elinor will probably be settled for life. We shall miss her, but she will be happy.”
“Oh! Mama, how will we manage without her?”

“My love, it will hardly be a separation at all. We shall live only a few miles apart and see each other every day of our lives. You will gain a brother—a real, loving brother. I could not think more highly of Edward's heart. But you look serious, Marianne. Do you disapprove of your sister's choice?”

“Perhaps,” Marianne said, “I do find it a little surprising. Edward is very kind, and I am deeply fond of him. But still—he is not quite the sort of young man—something is missing. His appearance is not striking. He has none of the grace I would expect in a man who could win my sister's serious affection. His eyes lack that spirit, that fire, which immediately reveals goodness and intelligence. And besides all this, Mama, I am afraid he has no real taste. Music hardly seems to interest him. He admires Elinor's drawings very much, but not as someone who understands their value. For all the attention he gives her while she draws, it is obvious that he actually knows nothing about it. He admires them as a lover, not as a connoisseur. To satisfy me, a man must be both. I could never be happy with someone whose taste differed from mine in any respect. He must share every feeling I have. The same books and the same music must enchant us both. Oh! Mama, how lifeless and flat Edward sounded when he read to us last night! I felt so terribly for my sister. Yet she listened so calmly that she hardly seemed to notice. I could scarcely stay in my seat. Those beautiful lines, which have so often almost driven me wild, spoken with such unshakable calm, such dreadful indifference!”
“He would certainly have done greater justice to clear, elegant prose. I thought that at the time. But you insisted on giving him Cowper.”

“But Mama, if Cowper cannot stir him! Still, we must make allowances for differences in taste. Elinor does not feel as I do, so she may overlook it and be happy with him. But if I had loved him, hearing him read with so little feeling would have broken my heart. Mama, the more I learn about the world, the more certain I become that I shall never meet a man I can truly love. I demand so much! He must possess all Edward's virtues, and his appearance and manners must add every possible charm to his goodness.”

“Remember, my love, you are not yet seventeen. It is far too early to give up hope of such happiness. Why should you be less fortunate than your mother? In just one respect, my Marianne, may your fate differ from hers!”

chapters.title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: “What a shame, Elinor,” Marianne said, “that Edward has no appreciation of drawing.”

“No appreciation of drawing!” Elinor replied. “Why would you think that? It is true that he does not draw himself, but he takes great pleasure in other people's work. I assure you, he has plenty of natural taste, though he has never had the chance to develop it. If he had been given an opportunity to learn, I believe he would have drawn very well. He has so little confidence in his judgment on these subjects that he is always reluctant to express an opinion about a picture. But his taste has a natural soundness and simplicity that generally leads him to judge things quite correctly.”

Afraid of giving offence, Marianne dropped the subject. Still, the approval Elinor described him giving other people's drawings fell far short of the ecstatic delight which, in Marianne's view, alone deserved to be called taste. Though she smiled inwardly at the mistake, she respected her sister for the blind affection for Edward that had led her into it.

“I hope, Marianne,” Elinor went on, “you do not think he lacks taste in general. In fact, I believe I can say you cannot think so. You are perfectly warm towards him, and if you held that opinion, I am sure you could never manage to be polite to him.”
Marianne scarcely knew how to answer. Nothing would have persuaded her to hurt her sister's feelings, but saying something she did not believe was equally impossible. At last she replied:

“Do not take offence, Elinor, if my praise does not match your opinion of him in every respect. I have had fewer chances than you to judge the finer tendencies of his mind, his tastes and preferences. But I think as highly as anyone could of his kindness and good sense. I consider him worthy and lovable in every way.”
“I am certain,” Elinor replied with a smile, “that even his closest friends could ask for no better praise than that. I cannot see how you could speak of him with greater warmth.”
Marianne was delighted that it took so little to satisfy her sister.

“As for his intelligence and goodness,” Elinor continued, “I think nobody could doubt either after seeing him often enough to draw him into an open conversation. Only the shyness that so often keeps him silent can conceal how sound his understanding and principles are. You know him well enough to recognise his real worth. But circumstances have given me more opportunities than you to observe what you call the finer tendencies of his mind. He and I have sometimes spent a good deal of time together while you, out of the most loving concern, have been entirely occupied with Mama. I have seen much of him, considered his views, and heard his opinions on books and questions of taste. Taking everything together, I venture to say that he is well informed, takes enormous pleasure in reading, has a lively imagination, observes things accurately and sensibly, and possesses a refined, unspoilt taste. His abilities improve on acquaintance just as much as his manners and appearance do. At first his manner is certainly not striking. And you would scarcely call him handsome until you noticed the expression of his unusually fine eyes and the general gentleness of his face. Now that I know him so well, I really do think him handsome—or at least very nearly so. What do you say, Marianne?”
“If I do not think him handsome already, Elinor, I very soon shall. Once you tell me to love him as a brother, I shall see no more faults in his face than I now see in his heart.”

Elinor was startled by this declaration and regretted having allowed herself to speak so warmly about him. She knew how highly she thought of Edward. She believed he cared for her too, but needed to be more certain before she could welcome Marianne's confidence in their attachment. She knew that whatever Marianne and her mother guessed one moment, they believed the next. For them, wishing became hoping, and hoping became expecting. She tried to explain the actual situation to her sister.
“I am not trying to deny,” she said, “that I think very highly of him—that I have great respect for him, that I like him.”
At this Marianne broke out in indignation—
“Respect him! Like him! How cold-hearted you are, Elinor! Oh! Worse than cold-hearted—you are ashamed of having warmer feelings. Say those words again, and I shall leave the room at once.”

Elinor could not help laughing. “Forgive me,” she said. “Please believe that I meant no offence to you by describing my own feelings so calmly. You may believe they are stronger than I have said. In short, believe them as strong as his worth and my suspicion—my hope—that he cares for me could reasonably justify, without foolishness or a lack of caution. But you must not believe anything beyond that. I am by no means certain of his affection. At times I doubt how far it goes. Until I know his feelings fully, you cannot be surprised that I wish to avoid encouraging my own by imagining or calling them more than they are. In my heart I have little doubt—hardly any—that he prefers me. But we must consider more than his wishes. He is very far from financially independent. We cannot know what his mother is really like. But Fanny's occasional accounts of her behaviour and opinions have never made us think her kind. And unless I am greatly mistaken, Edward himself knows how many obstacles he would face if he wanted to marry a woman with neither a large fortune nor high social rank.”
Marianne was astonished to discover how far she and her mother had let their imaginations run ahead of the facts.

“So you really are not engaged to him!” she said. “But surely it will happen very soon. Meanwhile, the delay will bring two advantages. I shall not lose you quite so quickly, and Edward will have more time to develop his natural taste for your favourite occupation—a taste that must be absolutely essential to your future happiness. Oh! How delightful it would be if your talent inspired him to learn to draw himself!”

Elinor had told her sister what she truly thought. She could not regard her affection for Edward as having so promising a future as Marianne supposed. At times he seemed low-spirited in a way that, if it did not indicate indifference, suggested something almost equally discouraging. If he doubted her feelings for him, that need cause no more than uneasiness. It was unlikely to explain the dejection he so often showed. A more plausible explanation was his dependence on his mother, which prevented him from acting on his affection. Elinor knew that his mother neither made his present home comfortable nor gave him any confidence that he could establish a home of his own unless he strictly followed her ambitious plans for him. Knowing this, Elinor could not feel at ease. She was far from counting on the outcome of his preference that her mother and sister still took for granted. Indeed, the longer they spent together, the less certain she became of what he felt. Sometimes, for a few painful minutes, she believed it was nothing beyond friendship.

Whatever the true extent of his affection, his sister noticed enough to make her uneasy, and, more commonly still, rude. She seized the first opportunity to insult her mother-in-law on the subject. She spoke so pointedly about her brother's great expectations, Mrs. Ferrars's determination that both her sons should marry well, and the danger to any young woman who tried to entrap him, that Mrs. Dashwood could neither pretend not to understand nor attempt to remain calm. She answered with unmistakable contempt and immediately left the room. Whatever inconvenience or expense a sudden move might bring, she resolved that her beloved Elinor would not endure another week of such insinuations.

While she was in this mood, a letter arrived by post containing a particularly timely proposal. A relative of her own, a gentleman of wealth and standing in Devonshire, offered her a small house at a very modest rent. He had written the letter himself, with a sincere wish to help. He understood that she needed a home. The house he offered was only a cottage, but if she liked its location, he assured her that he would have anything done to it that she thought necessary. After describing the house and garden, he warmly urged her to bring her daughters to Barton Park, where he lived. From there she could judge for herself whether alterations might make Barton Cottage comfortable enough for her; the two houses were in the same parish. He seemed truly eager to accommodate them. The friendliness of the whole letter could not fail to please his cousin, especially just then, when she was suffering from the cold and unfeeling behaviour of much closer relations. She needed no time for thought or further inquiries. Her decision formed as she read. Only hours earlier, Barton's position in Devonshire, so far from Sussex, would have outweighed every possible advantage it offered. Now the distance was its greatest attraction. Leaving Norland's neighbourhood no longer seemed a hardship. It was something to long for, a blessing compared with the misery of remaining her daughter-in-law's guest. Even leaving that beloved place for ever would hurt less than living in it, or visiting it, while such a woman was its mistress. She immediately wrote to thank Sir John Middleton for his kindness and accept his offer. Then she hurried to show her daughters both letters, so that she could secure their approval before sending her reply.

Elinor had always thought it wiser to settle some distance from Norland rather than remain in the immediate circle of their present acquaintances. On that point, therefore, she could hardly oppose her mother's decision to move to Devonshire. Sir John's description also made the house sound so modest in size, and its rent so unusually low, that she had no grounds for objecting to either. The plan did not appeal to her imagination, and it took them farther from Norland than she wished. Nevertheless, she made no attempt to discourage her mother from sending her acceptance.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: As soon as her reply was sent, Mrs. Dashwood allowed herself the pleasure of telling her stepson and his wife that she had found a house. She would inconvenience them only until it was ready for her to occupy. They listened in surprise. Mrs. John Dashwood said nothing, but her husband politely hoped that she would not be moving far from Norland. Mrs. Dashwood took great satisfaction in announcing that she was going to Devonshire. At this Edward turned quickly towards her. With surprise and distress in his voice, which she had no difficulty interpreting, he repeated, “Devonshire! Are you really going there? So far away! And to what part?” She explained its location: it lay less than four miles north of Exeter.

“It is only a cottage,” she continued, “but I hope to welcome many of my friends there. We can easily add a room or two. If my friends can manage the journey all that way to see me, I am sure I can manage to make room for them.”

She ended by warmly inviting Mr. and Mrs. John Dashwood to visit her at Barton, and invited Edward with still greater affection. Her recent conversation with her daughter-in-law had made her determined to remain at Norland no longer than necessary. But on the chief point Mrs. John Dashwood had intended to press, it had had no effect whatever. She was as little inclined as ever to separate Edward and Elinor. By pointedly inviting her daughter-in-law's brother, she meant to show how completely she disregarded that lady's opposition to the match.

Mr. John Dashwood repeatedly told his mother how deeply sorry he was that she had chosen a house so far from Norland that he could not help her move her furniture. His conscience was genuinely troubled: this arrangement made impossible the very service to which he had reduced his promise to his father. Everything was sent round by sea. The belongings consisted chiefly of household linen, silver, china, and books, together with Marianne's handsome pianoforte. Mrs. John Dashwood watched the packages leave with a sigh. She could not help thinking it unfair that Mrs. Dashwood, whose income would be so tiny beside theirs, should own any fine furniture at all.

Mrs. Dashwood rented the cottage for a year. It came furnished, and she could move in immediately. Neither side found any difficulty in the agreement. Before leaving for the west, she needed only to arrange the removal or disposal of her belongings at Norland and decide on her future household. As she acted extremely quickly in anything that interested her, this was soon accomplished. The horses her husband had left her had been sold shortly after his death. An opportunity now arose to sell the carriage too, and at her eldest daughter's earnest urging she agreed to part with it. Left to her own wishes, she would have kept it for her children's comfort. But Elinor's prudence prevailed. It was also Elinor's good sense that restricted them to three servants: two maids and a man, quickly selected from the servants who had formed their household at Norland.

The man and one maid went to Devonshire at once to prepare the house for their mistress. Mrs. Dashwood had never met Lady Middleton, and preferred going straight to the cottage to staying as a guest at Barton Park. She trusted Sir John's description so completely that she felt no curiosity to inspect the place before entering it as her own home. Her daughter-in-law's obvious pleasure at the prospect of her departure kept her eagerness to leave Norland undiminished. That pleasure was barely concealed beneath a cold invitation to postpone the journey. This was a particularly fitting moment for her stepson to fulfil his promise to his father. Having failed to do so when he first inherited the estate, he might reasonably regard their departure from his house as the best occasion to act. But Mrs. Dashwood soon began to abandon every such hope. The general direction of his conversation convinced her that his help extended no further than supporting them for six months at Norland. He spoke so often of rising household expenses, and of the endless and incalculable demands upon the purse of any man of standing, that he seemed to need more money himself rather than intend to give any away.

Within only a few weeks of Sir John Middleton's first letter reaching Norland, arrangements at their future home were sufficiently complete for Mrs. Dashwood and her daughters to set out on their journey.

They shed many tears in saying their final farewells to a place they loved so much. “Dear, dear Norland!” Marianne said as she walked alone in front of the house on their last evening there. “When shall I stop mourning for you! When shall I learn to feel at home anywhere else! Oh! Happy house, if only you knew what I suffer as I look at you from this spot, where perhaps I shall never stand to see you again! And you, familiar trees! You will go on just the same. Not a leaf will wither because we have left, nor a branch stop moving because we can no longer watch you! No, you will remain unchanged, unaware of the pleasure or the sorrow you cause, knowing nothing of any change in those who walk beneath your shade! But who will be left to enjoy you?”

chapters.title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: They were too melancholy during the first part of the journey to find it anything but tedious and unpleasant. As they neared its end, however, their interest in the landscape of their new home began to overcome their sadness. The sight of Barton Valley as they entered it cheered them. It was a pleasant, fertile place, with plenty of trees and rich pasture. After following its winding course for more than a mile, they reached their house. Its entire front grounds consisted of a small grassy courtyard, entered through a neat little gate.

Considered as a house, Barton Cottage was comfortable and compact, though small. Considered as a cottage, it had serious shortcomings: its shape was regular, its roof tiled, its shutters were not green, and no honeysuckle covered the walls. A narrow passage ran straight through the building to the back garden. On either side of the entrance stood a sitting room, each about sixteen feet square, with the service rooms and staircase beyond. Four bedrooms and two attic rooms completed the house. It had been built fairly recently and was in good condition. Beside Norland, how poor and small it was! But the tears that memory brought as they entered soon dried. The servants' delight at their arrival cheered them, and each resolved to look happy for the others' sake. It was the very beginning of September, and the weather was fine. Seeing the place first in such favourable conditions gave them a good impression that did much to secure their lasting affection for it.

The house was well situated. High hills rose directly behind it and quite close on either side. Some were open downland; others held cultivated fields and woods. Most of Barton village stood on one of these hills, making a pleasant view from the cottage windows. In front, the outlook was wider, taking in the whole valley and stretching into the country beyond. The hills around the cottage closed the valley at this end. Between two of the steepest, it opened out again in another direction and under another name.

On the whole, Mrs. Dashwood was pleased with the house's size and furnishings. Her former way of life made many additions to the furniture seem indispensable, but adding and improving were pleasures to her. For now, she had enough ready money to supply everything needed to make the rooms more elegant. “As for the house itself,” she said, “of course it is too small for our family. Still, we shall make ourselves reasonably comfortable for the present, since it is too late in the year to make improvements. Perhaps in spring, if I have plenty of money—as I dare say I shall—we can consider building. Both these parlours are too small for the gatherings of friends I hope we shall often have here. I have thought of adding the passage to one room, perhaps with part of the other, and leaving what remains of that second room as an entrance. With a new drawing room, which could easily be added, and a bedroom and attic above it, that would make a very snug little cottage. I wish the stairs were handsomer. But one cannot expect everything—though I suppose widening them would not be difficult. In spring I shall see how much money I have to spare, and we shall plan our improvements accordingly.”

Meanwhile, until all these alterations could be paid for out of savings from five hundred a year, made by a woman who had never saved anything in her life, they had the sense to be content with the house as it stood. Each occupied herself with arranging her own affairs and trying to make a home by placing books and other belongings around her. Marianne's pianoforte was unpacked and put in its proper place; Elinor's drawings were hung on the sitting-room walls.

Soon after breakfast the next day, these occupations were interrupted by their landlord. He had come to welcome them to Barton and offer anything from his own house and garden that theirs might still lack. Sir John Middleton was a good-looking man of about forty. He had visited them at Stanhill, but too long ago for his young cousins to remember him. His face was full of good humour, and his manner as friendly as his letter. Their arrival seemed to give him genuine pleasure, and their comfort to be a matter of genuine concern. He spoke at length of his wish for them to be on the closest social terms with his family. He urged them so warmly to dine at Barton Park every day until they were better settled that, although his persistence went beyond the bounds of politeness, it could not offend them. Nor did his kindness end with words. Within an hour of his leaving, a large basket of vegetables and fruit arrived from the park; before the day was over, a gift of game followed. He also insisted on having all their letters carried to and from the post, and would not be refused the pleasure of sending them his newspaper every day.

Lady Middleton had sent a very polite message through him. She intended to call on Mrs. Dashwood as soon as she could be sure her visit would cause no inconvenience. An equally polite invitation was sent back, and her ladyship was introduced to them the following day.

Naturally they were eager to meet someone on whom so much of their comfort at Barton would depend. Her elegant appearance encouraged their hopes. Lady Middleton was no more than twenty-six or twenty-seven, with a handsome face, a tall and striking figure, and a graceful manner. She possessed all the elegance her husband lacked. A share of his openness and warmth would have improved her manners, however. Her visit lasted long enough to lessen their first admiration. It revealed that, although perfectly well bred, she was reserved and cold, and had nothing to say beyond the most ordinary question or remark.

There was no shortage of conversation, however. Sir John was very talkative, and Lady Middleton had wisely brought their eldest child, a fine little boy of about six. This supplied the ladies with a subject to return to whenever conversation became desperate. They had to ask his name and age, admire his looks, and put questions to him which his mother answered. Meanwhile he clung to her with his head lowered, much to her ladyship's surprise. She wondered why he was so shy in company when he could make quite enough noise at home. A child should accompany every formal visit as a reserve supply of conversation. On this occasion, deciding whether the boy most resembled his father or his mother, and precisely how he resembled each, occupied ten minutes. Naturally everyone disagreed, and everyone was astonished by everyone else's opinion.
The Dashwoods would soon have an opportunity to debate the appearance of the remaining children. Sir John refused to leave until they had promised to dine at the park the next day.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Barton Park stood about half a mile from the cottage. The ladies had passed close to it while travelling through the valley, but a jutting hill hid it from their view at home. It was a large, handsome house, and the Middletons' way of living was equally hospitable and elegant. The hospitality pleased Sir John; the elegance pleased his wife. They almost always had friends staying with them, and entertained more company of every sort than any other family nearby. Both needed this for their happiness. Different as they were in temperament and behaviour, they closely resembled each other in a complete lack of talent and taste. Without the occupations society provided, their activities were extremely limited. Sir John was a sportsman; Lady Middleton was a mother. He hunted and shot; she indulged her children. These were their only resources. Lady Middleton had the advantage of being able to spoil her children throughout the year, while Sir John's separate pursuits occupied only half of it. Constant engagements at home and elsewhere, however, made up for everything nature and education had failed to supply. They kept Sir John in good spirits and gave his wife opportunities to display her good breeding.

Lady Middleton prided herself on the elegance of her table and every detail of her household arrangements. Gratifying that vanity gave her the greatest pleasure she took in their parties. Sir John's enjoyment of company was much more genuine. He loved gathering more young people around him than his house could hold, and the more noise they made, the happier he was. He was a blessing to all the younger people in the neighbourhood. In summer he constantly organised parties to eat cold ham and chicken outdoors. In winter he gave enough private balls to satisfy any young lady who was not afflicted with the insatiable appetite of fifteen.

A new family arriving in the neighbourhood always delighted him, and he was pleased in every respect with the occupants he had obtained for his Barton cottage. The Miss Dashwoods were young, pretty, and natural. That was enough to win his approval: a pretty girl needed only to be unaffected for her mind to become as captivating as her looks. His friendly nature made him happy to help people whose present circumstances, compared with their past, could be considered unfortunate. In being kind to his cousins, he therefore enjoyed the true satisfaction of a good heart. In putting a household composed entirely of women into his cottage, he enjoyed all the satisfaction of a sportsman. For a sportsman, though he values only men who share his sporting interests, rarely wishes to encourage those interests by letting them live on his own estate.

Sir John met Mrs. Dashwood and her daughters at the door and welcomed them to Barton Park with entirely sincere warmth. As he led them to the drawing room, he repeated to the young ladies his regret, already expressed the day before, that he had been unable to find any lively young men to meet them. They would see only one other gentleman, he said: a particular friend staying at the park, neither very young nor very merry. He hoped they would forgive such a small gathering, and promised it would never happen again. That morning he had called on several families in the hope of adding to the party. But with moonlight making evening travel easy, everyone was full of engagements. Luckily, Lady Middleton's mother had arrived at Barton within the past hour. She was a very cheerful, agreeable woman, so he hoped the young ladies would not find things quite as dull as they might expect. The young ladies and their mother were perfectly content with two complete strangers in the company, and wished for no more.

Lady Middleton's mother, Mrs. Jennings, was a merry, good-natured, stout elderly woman. She talked a great deal, seemed very happy, and was rather vulgar. Full of jokes and laughter, she had made numerous witty remarks about lovers and husbands before dinner ended. She hoped they had not left their hearts in Sussex, and pretended to see them blush whether they did or not. Marianne resented this for her sister's sake. She watched Elinor to see how she endured the teasing, with an intensity that caused Elinor far more discomfort than Mrs. Jennings's ordinary jokes could have done.

Sir John's friend, Colonel Brandon, seemed no better suited by similarity of manners to be his friend than Lady Middleton was to be his wife, or Mrs. Jennings to be Lady Middleton's mother. He was quiet and serious. His appearance was nevertheless quite pleasing, despite being, in Marianne and Margaret's opinion, an absolute old bachelor: he was on the far side of thirty-five. His face was not handsome, but it showed intelligence, and his manner was especially gentlemanly.

Nobody in the party had much to recommend them as companions for the Dashwoods. Yet Lady Middleton's cold dullness was so particularly off-putting that beside it Colonel Brandon's seriousness seemed interesting, and even Sir John and his mother-in-law's boisterous merriment had its attractions. Lady Middleton seemed to take pleasure in nothing until her four noisy children entered after dinner. They pulled at her, tore her clothes, and ended every conversation that was not about themselves.

In the evening, when the company discovered Marianne's musical abilities, they asked her to play. The instrument was unlocked, everyone prepared to be delighted, and Marianne, who sang very well, performed at their request most of the songs Lady Middleton had brought with her on her marriage. Perhaps they had lain in the same place on the pianoforte ever since. Her ladyship had celebrated her wedding by giving up music, although her mother said she had played extremely well, and she herself claimed to be very fond of it.

Marianne's performance received enthusiastic applause. Sir John loudly admired every song when it ended, and talked just as loudly to the others throughout it. Lady Middleton repeatedly reproved him, wondered how anybody could turn their attention from music for an instant, and asked Marianne to sing a particular song she had just finished. Colonel Brandon alone listened without going into raptures. The only compliment he offered was his attention. For that Marianne felt a respect which the others had quite reasonably forfeited through their shameless lack of taste. His enjoyment of music fell short of the ecstasy that alone could answer her own, but it deserved credit beside the others' dreadful insensitivity. She was reasonable enough to admit that a man of thirty-five might well have outlived all intensity of feeling and every exquisite capacity for pleasure. She was entirely willing to make whatever allowances humanity required for the colonel's advanced age.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Mrs. Jennings was a widow with a generous income settled on her at marriage. She had only two daughters and had lived to see both respectably married. Nothing therefore remained for her to do except marry off the rest of the world. She worked at this with all the energy her abilities allowed, missing no opportunity to plan weddings among the young people she knew. She was remarkably quick to discover attachments, and had enjoyed making many a young lady blush and feel important by hinting at her influence over a particular young man. This gift of perception enabled her, soon after arriving at Barton, to declare with certainty that Colonel Brandon was deeply in love with Marianne Dashwood. She suspected it on their very first evening together because he listened so attentively to Marianne's singing. When the Middletons returned the visit by dining at the cottage, his listening again settled the matter. It must be true; she was entirely convinced. They would make an excellent match: he was rich, and she was beautiful. Ever since her connection with Sir John had brought Colonel Brandon into her acquaintance, Mrs. Jennings had wanted to see him well married. And she was always eager to find a good husband for every pretty girl.

The immediate benefit to herself was substantial, since the discovery provided an endless supply of jokes at both their expense. At the park she teased the colonel; at the cottage she teased Marianne. He probably cared nothing about the jokes, so far as they concerned only himself. Marianne at first could not understand them. Once she understood their point, she scarcely knew whether to laugh at their absurdity or condemn their impertinence. She thought them an unfeeling comment on the colonel's great age and his lonely situation as an old bachelor.

Mrs. Dashwood could not consider a man five years younger than herself quite as ancient as her daughter's youthful imagination made him. She ventured to suggest that Mrs. Jennings probably had no intention of making fun of his age.

“But Mama, even if you do not think the accusation deliberately unkind, you must admit how absurd it is. Colonel Brandon is certainly younger than Mrs. Jennings, but he is old enough to be my father. If he ever had enough spirit to fall in love, he must have outlived such feelings long ago. It is too ridiculous! When can a man be safe from jokes like these, if age and infirmity offer him no protection?”

“Infirmity!” Elinor said. “Do you call Colonel Brandon infirm? I can quite understand that he seems much older to you than to Mama. But surely you cannot persuade yourself that he has lost the use of his limbs!”
“Did you not hear him complain of rheumatism? And is that not the most common affliction of advancing age?”
“My dearest child,” her mother said, laughing, “by that reasoning you must live in constant fear of my decline. It must seem miraculous to you that I have survived to the advanced age of forty.”

“Mama, you are being unfair to me. I know perfectly well that Colonel Brandon is not yet old enough for his friends to fear losing him through natural causes. He may live another twenty years. But thirty-five has no business with marriage.”

“Perhaps,” Elinor said, “thirty-five and seventeen ought not to have any business with marrying each other. But if there happened to be a woman still single at twenty-seven, I should not consider his being thirty-five any reason against his marrying her.”

“A woman of twenty-seven,” Marianne said after a brief pause, “can never expect to feel or inspire love again. If her home is uncomfortable or she has little money, I can imagine her agreeing to act as a nurse in return for a wife's maintenance and security. There would therefore be nothing unsuitable in his marrying such a woman. It would be an arrangement of convenience, and society would be satisfied. I should not call it a marriage at all, but that would not matter. To me it would seem simply a business exchange, each party hoping to profit at the other's expense.”

“I know it would be impossible,” Elinor replied, “to persuade you that a woman of twenty-seven might feel anything close enough to love for a man of thirty-five to make her want him as a companion. But I must object to your sentencing Colonel Brandon and his wife to permanent confinement in a sickroom merely because yesterday, on a very cold, damp day, he happened to mention a slight rheumatic pain in one shoulder.”
“But he spoke about flannel waistcoats,” Marianne said. “And to me a flannel waistcoat always means aches, cramps, rheumatism, and every other complaint that can trouble the old and feeble.”

“If he had only been suffering from a violent fever, you would not have despised him half so much. Admit it, Marianne: do you not find something appealing in the flushed cheeks, sunken eyes, and racing pulse of a fever?”

Soon afterwards, when Elinor left the room, Marianne said, “Mama, I have a fear about illness that I cannot keep from you. I am sure Edward Ferrars is unwell. We have been here nearly a fortnight, and still he does not come. Nothing but real illness could explain such an extraordinary delay. What else could keep him at Norland?”

“Did you expect him to come so soon?” Mrs. Dashwood asked. “I did not. Indeed, if I have felt any anxiety about it, it has been because I remember how little pleasure or eagerness he sometimes showed in accepting my invitation when I spoke of his coming to Barton. Is Elinor already expecting him?”
“I have not mentioned it to her, but naturally she must be.”

“I rather think you are mistaken. Yesterday, when I spoke to her about buying a new fireplace grate for the spare bedroom, she said there was no immediate hurry, since we were unlikely to need the room for some time.”

“How strange! What can it mean! But their entire behaviour towards each other has been impossible to explain! Their last farewells were so cold, so calm! Their conversation on their final evening together was so lifeless! Edward said goodbye to Elinor exactly as he did to me, offering us both the good wishes of a loving brother. Twice on that last morning I deliberately left them alone together, and each time, for no understandable reason, he followed me out. And when Elinor left Norland and Edward, she did not cry as I did. Even now she never loses her self-control. When does she seem miserable or low-spirited? When does she try to escape company, or seem restless and unhappy in it?”

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: The Dashwoods were now reasonably comfortable in their settled life at Barton. The house, garden, and everything around them had become familiar. They had resumed the everyday occupations that had given Norland half its charm, enjoying them far more than they had been able to enjoy anything there since their father's death. Sir John Middleton called every day during their first fortnight. Unused to seeing much activity in his own home, he could not hide his amazement at finding them always busy.

Apart from the people at Barton Park, they had few visitors. Sir John repeatedly urged them to meet more of their neighbours and assured them that his carriage was always at their disposal. But Mrs. Dashwood's independent spirit was stronger than her wish to provide company for her children. She firmly refused to visit any family beyond walking distance. Few lived close enough, and not all of those could be approached. On one of their first walks, the girls had found an old, respectable-looking mansion about a mile and a half from the cottage, along the narrow, winding Allenham valley that branched from Barton Valley as already described. It reminded them a little of Norland, stirring their imaginations and making them wish to know it better. On asking about it, however, they learned that its owner, an elderly lady of excellent reputation, was unfortunately too frail to go into society and never left home.

The surrounding countryside offered beautiful walks in every direction. From almost every cottage window, the high downs invited them to enjoy the wonderful fresh air on their summits. These provided a pleasant alternative whenever mud in the valleys cut off access to the still greater beauties below. One memorable morning, Marianne and Margaret set out towards one of these hills. Patches of sunshine in a showery sky drew them outside, and after two days of steady rain they could no longer bear being shut indoors. The weather did not tempt the other two away from their drawing and reading, despite Marianne's insistence that the day would remain fine and every threatening cloud would drift away from their hills. The two younger girls therefore went out together.

They climbed the downs merrily, congratulating themselves on their good judgment whenever blue sky appeared. When the invigorating gusts of a strong south-westerly wind struck their faces, they pitied the fears that had kept their mother and Elinor from sharing such delightful sensations.
“Can there be any happiness in the world,” Marianne said, “greater than this? Margaret, we shall walk here for at least two hours.”

Margaret agreed. They continued into the wind, laughing with delight as they struggled against it for another twenty minutes or so. Then the clouds suddenly joined overhead, and driving rain struck them full in the face. Disappointed and surprised, they had to turn back, unwilling as they were, since the nearest shelter was their own house. One consolation remained, and the urgency of the moment made it more justifiable than usual: they could run as fast as possible down the steep hillside that led straight to their garden gate.
They began to run. Marianne took the lead at first, but a misstep suddenly brought her down. Margaret could not stop herself to help; her momentum carried her on, and she reached the bottom safely.

A gentleman carrying a gun, with two pointers bounding around him, was coming up the hill only a few yards from Marianne when she fell. He put his gun down and ran to help. She had got up, but had twisted her foot in the fall and could scarcely stand. He offered assistance. Seeing that embarrassment made her refuse the help her situation required, he lifted her into his arms without further delay and carried her down the hill. He passed through the garden gate, which Margaret had left open, and took her straight into the house, where Margaret had only just arrived. He did not let her go until he had placed her in a parlour chair.

Elinor and her mother rose in astonishment at their entrance. Both watched him with open surprise and a private admiration, equally prompted by his appearance. He apologised for intruding and explained what had happened, with such openness and grace that his voice and expression added further charm to his unusually handsome looks. Even if he had been old, ugly, and vulgar, any kindness to her child would have secured Mrs. Dashwood's gratitude and goodwill. But youth, beauty, and elegance gave the action a special appeal that touched her feelings directly.

She thanked him repeatedly and, with her usual sweetness, invited him to sit down. He declined because he was wet and muddy. Mrs. Dashwood then begged to know the name of the person to whom she was indebted. He replied that it was Willoughby and that he was staying at Allenham. He hoped she would allow him the honour of calling from there the next day to ask after Miss Dashwood. Permission was readily given. He then departed in the middle of a heavy downpour, making himself still more interesting by doing so.

His masculine good looks and exceptional grace immediately became the subject of general admiration. The teasing his gallantry brought upon Marianne was made particularly lively by his attractive appearance. She herself had seen less of him than anyone else. The confusion that had flooded her face with colour when he lifted her had prevented her from looking at him after they entered the house. But she had seen enough to join the others' admiration with all the energy she always brought to praise. His looks and bearing matched everything her imagination had pictured in the hero of a favourite story. Carrying her inside without preliminary formalities showed a quickness of decision that especially pleased her. Everything about him was interesting. His name was pleasing, he lived in their favourite village, and she soon discovered that nothing a man could wear was more becoming than a shooting jacket. Her imagination was occupied, her thoughts were delightful, and the pain of her sprained ankle went unnoticed.

Sir John called as soon as the next spell of fair weather that morning allowed him outside. They told him about Marianne's accident and eagerly asked whether he knew a gentleman named Willoughby at Allenham.
“Willoughby!” Sir John exclaimed. “Is he here in the neighbourhood? Well, that is good news! I shall ride over tomorrow and invite him to dinner on Thursday.”
“Then you are acquainted with him,” Mrs. Dashwood said.
“Acquainted with him! Of course I am. Why, he comes down here every year.”
“And what kind of young man would you say he is?”
“One of the best fellows that ever lived, I assure you. A very good shot, and you will not find a bolder rider anywhere in England.”
“Is that all you can tell us about him?” Marianne exclaimed indignantly. “What are his manners like when you know him better? What are his interests, his talents, his gifts?”
Sir John looked rather puzzled.

“Upon my soul,” he said, “I cannot tell you much about all that. But he is a pleasant, good-natured fellow and owns the finest little black pointer bitch I have ever seen. Did he have her with him today?”
But Marianne was no more able to tell him the colour of Mr. Willoughby's pointer than he was to describe the finer shades of Mr. Willoughby's mind.
“But who is he?” Elinor asked. “Where is he from? Does he own a house at Allenham?”

On this subject Sir John had more definite information. He explained that Mr. Willoughby owned no property in the neighbourhood. He stayed there only when visiting the old lady at Allenham Court, a relation whose property he was to inherit. He added, “Yes, indeed, Miss Dashwood, he is well worth catching, I can tell you. Besides all that, he has a pretty little estate of his own in Somersetshire. If I were you, I would not leave him to my younger sister, for all this falling down hills. Miss Marianne must not expect to keep every man for herself. Brandon will grow jealous if she is not careful.”

“I do not think,” Mrs. Dashwood said with a good-humoured smile, “that Mr. Willoughby will suffer any inconvenience from either of my daughters trying to do what you call catching him. They have not been brought up to regard that as an occupation. Men are quite safe with us, however rich they may be. Still, I am glad to learn from your account that he is a respectable young man whose acquaintance we may properly welcome.”

“I believe he is as good a fellow as ever lived,” Sir John repeated. “At a little dance at the park last Christmas, I remember him dancing from eight in the evening until four in the morning without sitting down once.”
“Did he really?” Marianne exclaimed, her eyes shining. “And did he dance gracefully, with spirit?”
“Yes, and at eight he was up again to ride out to the hunt.”
“That is what I admire; that is how a young man ought to be. Whatever he takes up, his enthusiasm should have no limits and leave him unaware of being tired.”
“Yes, yes, I can see what will happen,” Sir John said. “I see it already. Now you will be setting your cap at him and forgetting poor Brandon entirely.”

“That expression, Sir John,” Marianne answered heatedly, “is one I particularly dislike. I detest all the worn-out phrases people use when they mean to be witty. ‘Setting one's cap at a man’ and ‘making a conquest’ are the worst of them. Their implications are coarse and ungenerous. Even if the wording could ever have been thought clever, time has long since worn away every trace of ingenuity.”
Sir John understood very little of this rebuke. He laughed as heartily as though he understood it perfectly, however, and then answered:

“Yes, I dare say you will make plenty of conquests, one way or another. Poor Brandon! He is quite smitten already. And I can tell you that he is well worth setting your cap at, despite all this tumbling about and spraining ankles.”

chapters.title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: Willoughby, whom Margaret called Marianne's preserver with more elegance than accuracy, arrived early the next morning to ask after her in person. Mrs. Dashwood welcomed him with more than politeness. Sir John's account of him and her own gratitude inspired real warmth. Everything that happened during the visit confirmed the intelligence, elegance, mutual affection, and comfortable home life of the family an accident had introduced to him. Their personal attractions had needed no second visit to establish themselves.

Miss Dashwood had a delicate complexion, regular features, and a remarkably pretty figure. Marianne was more beautiful still. Her figure, though less perfectly proportioned than her sister's, was taller and more striking. Her face was so lovely that when the usual language of praise called her a beautiful girl, truth was less violently abused than it generally is. Her skin was very brown, but its clear quality made her complexion unusually brilliant. All her features were good; her smile was sweet and winning. Her very dark eyes held a life, a spirit, and an eagerness that could hardly be seen without pleasure. At first she kept their expression from Willoughby, embarrassed by the memory of his assistance. But the embarrassment faded and she recovered her composure. She saw that he combined a gentleman's perfect breeding with openness and liveliness. Above all, she heard him declare his passionate love of music and dancing. Then she gave him such a look of approval that he directed the greater part of his conversation to her for the rest of the visit.

Mentioning any favourite pastime was enough to set her talking. She could not stay silent on such subjects, and discussed them without shyness or reserve. They quickly discovered a shared love of dancing and music, founded on a general agreement in everything concerning either. Encouraged to explore his opinions further, she began asking about books. She introduced her favourite authors and spoke of them with such rapturous pleasure that a young man of twenty-five would have needed to be insensible indeed not to become an immediate admirer of their works, however little he had valued them before. Their tastes were strikingly similar. They adored the same books and the same passages. If any difference emerged, or any objection arose, it survived only until she could display the force of her arguments and the brightness of her eyes. He agreed with every judgment she made and caught all her enthusiasm. Long before the visit ended, they were talking with the ease of people who had known each other for years.

“Well, Marianne,” Elinor said as soon as he had gone, “I think you have done quite well for a single morning. You have already established Mr. Willoughby's views on nearly every important subject. You know what he thinks of Cowper and Scott. You are certain that he appreciates their beauties properly, and have every assurance that he admires Pope no more than he should. But how will you keep the acquaintance going after dealing with every possible topic so remarkably quickly? You will soon have used up all your favourite subjects. One more meeting will settle his opinions on picturesque beauty and second marriages, and then you will have nothing left to ask.”

“Elinor!” Marianne exclaimed. “Is that fair? Is it just? Are my ideas so limited? But I understand you. I have been too comfortable, too happy, too open. I have broken every conventional rule of proper behaviour. I was honest and sincere when I ought to have been reserved, lifeless, dull, and deceitful. If I had talked only about the weather and the roads, speaking once every ten minutes, you would have spared me this reproach.”

“My love,” her mother said, “you must not be angry with Elinor. She was only joking. I would scold her myself if she could possibly wish to spoil your pleasure in talking to our new friend.” Marianne's resentment vanished at once.

For his part, Willoughby showed every sign of enjoying their acquaintance that an obvious wish to develop it could provide. He visited daily. At first he came on the excuse of asking after Marianne, but the increasingly warm welcome made any excuse unnecessary before her complete recovery could make that particular excuse impossible. She had to remain indoors for several days, but no confinement had ever been less tiresome. Willoughby was able, quick in imagination, lively in spirits, and open and affectionate in his manners. He was exactly the man to win Marianne's heart. Along with all these qualities and his captivating appearance, he possessed a natural intensity of feeling, now stirred and strengthened by her example. This recommended him to her affection more powerfully than anything else.

Being with him gradually became her greatest delight. They read, talked, and sang together. He had considerable musical talent, and read aloud with all the feeling and animation that Edward had so unfortunately lacked.

Mrs. Dashwood considered him as faultless as Marianne did. Elinor could find only one thing to criticise: a habit that strongly resembled her sister's and especially delighted her, of saying too freely what he thought on every occasion, regardless of the people present or the circumstances. He formed and expressed opinions of others too quickly, sacrificed general courtesy to the pleasure of exclusive attention wherever his heart was engaged, and too readily dismissed the accepted rules of social behaviour. In all this he showed a lack of caution that Elinor could not approve, despite everything he and Marianne said in its defence.

Marianne now began to see that the despair which had seized her at sixteen and a half, of ever meeting a man who matched her ideal of perfection, had been hasty and unjustified. Willoughby was everything she had imagined, in that unhappy hour and in every happier one, as capable of winning her love. His behaviour suggested that his wish to win it was as strong as his ability to do so.

Her mother, too, whose mind had not entertained a single speculation about their marriage because of his prospects of wealth, began hoping for and expecting it before a week had passed. Privately she congratulated herself on gaining two such sons-in-law as Edward and Willoughby.

Colonel Brandon's preference for Marianne, discovered so early by his friends, first became visible to Elinor just as they stopped noticing it. Their attention and jokes had turned to his more fortunate rival. The teasing Brandon had endured before he felt any preference was withdrawn as soon as his feelings truly deserved the ridicule so justly attached to emotional sensitivity. Reluctantly, Elinor had to believe that her sister now really had inspired the affection Mrs. Jennings had previously assigned to him for her own amusement. A strong likeness of temperament might encourage Mr. Willoughby's love, but an equally striking difference of character did nothing to prevent Colonel Brandon's. Elinor observed this with concern. What hope could a quiet man of thirty-five have against a very lively one of twenty-five? Since she could not even wish him success, she sincerely wished he felt nothing. She liked him.
